title: North-east residents in with a chance of seeing Northern Lights as autumn equinox approaches

Coinciding with the autumn equinox, the darker nights create the perfect environment for a stunning Aurora Borealis display

Eilidh Farquhar

11:33, 22 Sep 2026

The skies of the north-east could soon turn technicolour as forecasters predict a possible Northern Lights sighting this week.

‌

Coinciding with the autumn equinox, the darker nights create the perfect environment for a stunning Aurora Borealis display. The Northern Lights is triggered by solar activity as charged particles from the sun interact with the Earth's magnetic field. This causes the gases in the upper atmosphere to transform into the spectacular light show.

‌

And while people often travel to different countries in the hopes of seeing the display, the perfect conditions could be round the corner here in Scotland.

‌

The Met Office is currently predicting that the next aurora sighting could perfectly align with the autumn equinox on Wednesday September 23, just as we are set to experience longer nights and chillier temperatures.

And while these darker conditions are ideal for a sighting of the Northern Lights on Wednesday and Thursday (September 24), people will only be able to view them if weather conditions are optimal, the Record reports.

The Met Office's aurora forecast reads: "Later on Wednesday 23rd September, fast winds are expected to arrive, bringing a chance of aurora sightings on Wednesday 23rd and Thursday 24th September across parts of Scotland, where skies are clear."

‌

According to weather maps, the night sky is expected to be clearer on Wednesday with only sporadic patches of cloud travelling across Scotland throughout the evening. However, cloud coverage is expected to be stronger on Thursday, with only pockets of clear spells dotted across the country.

With the seasons changing and nights getting longer, BBC weather presenter Simon King says that stargazers will now have a higher chance of spotting an aurora as this week is the "prime time" for the Northern Lights.

He explained: "Aurora spotting depends on a few factors. The first is we need longer and darker nights, and as we're now heading towards the autumn equinox, our nighttime will soon become longer than daylight.

‌

"Secondly, disturbances on the sun, known as sunspots, need to be pointing towards earth. It is these sunspots that can erupt, sending lots of energy into space, entering our atmosphere, interacting with oxygen and nitrogen to produce the colours we know as the aurora."

He also explained the way Earth is orientated towards the sun during the equinox, known as the Russell-McPherson effect, which can bring a peak in aurora viewings, heightening stargazers chances of viewing one.

September and October are some of the best months to view the Northern Lights, with the solar event being the most visible in Scotland out of the UK.

Top tips for viewing the Northern Lights

The Met Office has shared some tips on how to have the best chance of viewing the Northern Lights over the coming weeks and months.

  • Find dark, clear skies - light pollution and cloud cover can obscure the view.
  • Ideal locations - it is best to head to remote areas and look north, such as north-facing coasts.
  • Timing - the lights are most active around the equinoxes, but strong solar activity can bring surprises at other times of the year.
